newsitem.title: UK: New bureau to tackle European road haulage fraud.
newsitem.headline: New bureau to tackle European road haulage fraud.

text.p: The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) said Friday it is setting up a Transit Bureau to combat the growing problem of smuggling which takes advantage of disappearing road customs controls.
The ICC said goods are increasingly being fraudulent diverted while transported by road, with customs duty suspended, between nations in the Single European Market and across eastern Europe.
"The smuggling of goods by the continuous and uncontrollable use of false customs stamps is creating a crisis in the Transport Internationaux Routiers (TIR) carnet system," ICC said.
"The number of claims against the guarantee has increased from between three and 10 cases of dispute a day in 1991 to between 500 and 600 cases a day last year," the ICC stated.

Transit fraud was currently estimated to cost about ECU 4.5 billion a year. Fraud in the European Union mainly concerned goods which are subject to high taxation such as cigarettes or Common Agricultural Policy goods of high profitability due to tariff levels.
"The Transit Bureau will analyse information on transit crime to identify common factors, detect trends in criminal behavior and assist the industry to prevent frauds," the ICC said.

Data analysis will allow it to issue guidance notes for operators and the bureau will investigate specific cases of crime, particularly where national jurisdiction might provide a barrier to national enforcement bodies, the ICC said.

Executive director of commercial crime services at the ICC, Eric Ellen told Reuters: "The Transit Bureau is ready to go at a moment's notice. We have talked to governments and companies and are looking for 50 members for financial support."
The Transit Bureau will join other ICC initiatives to combat international crime affecting the business world.

It set up the International Maritime Bureau in the early 1980s and has since set up a Counterfeiting Intelligence Bureau to deal with the trade in counterfeit goods and a Commercial Crime Bureau to deal with banking fraud.
Like the ICC, they are non-profit making organisations with memberships including banks, lawyers, insurance companies, shipping and transport groups.
The ICC supports current action against fraud by the EU and Geneva-based Union Internationale des Routiers (IRU), which operates the TIR system.

But the introduction of individual guarantees by the EU for high risk goods was not sufficient on its own to prevent forgery. A commitment to computerise the transit system would also not directly help prevent fraud, the ICC claimed.
The IRU is also looking into setting up a crime database. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
